caption:
Microsoft has filed a patent application for AI that edits live video in near real time.
It would remove or replace a speaker's words and change their lip movements to match, based on each viewer's settings.

Would you want AI to clean up what speakers say on live TV?

threads_text: Microsoft filed a patent for AI that removes or replaces words in live video and reshapes the speaker's lips to match. Each viewer could hear a slightly different version of the same event. Helpful translation tool or deepfake machine?

slides.heading: Edited *as you speak*
paras: Microsoft filed a patent application for near real-time AI editing of live video and AR events, patent tracker Patentlyze found.
AI agents would remove or replace words, then adjust the speaker's face and mouth to match.

slides.heading: Goodbye *um* and y'all
paras: Examples include cutting filler words and stutters, and translating a live event into the viewer's language.
It could also drop slang like "y'all" or idioms like "bite the bullet", with replacements from internet search.

slides.heading: Everyone hears a *different speech*
paras: Edits would follow each viewer's profile, so two people could hear different versions of the same live event.
Critics warn it could fuel deepfakes. Microsoft has not commented.
slides.note: The filing says the original recording could be stored as a reference.

slides.hook: If AI starts rewriting live TV, you will want to know first. Follow for more.

paragraphs.text: Microsoft has filed a patent application for technology that would let artificial intelligence change what people say in live video, according to reports published on November 2 and 3, 2026. The filing describes "near real-time artificial intelligence (AI) enhancement of video or augmented reality (AR) presentations of live events," WION reported, citing patent tracker Patentlyze.

Under the system described in the application, AI agents identify spoken words or phrases that match a set of rules or a viewer's profile, then remove or replace them. The surrounding audio and video are edited almost instantly so that the change looks natural, and the speaker's face and mouth movements are adjusted to fit the new words, according to Digit.

Several examples appear in the application, according to the reports. One is live translation, where a viewer hears an event in a preferred language with lip movements adjusted to match. CXOToday reported that such translation could come with a delay of a few seconds. Another is cleaning up disfluencies, such as filler sounds, gasps and stutters.

The filing goes further than filler words. It lists the removal of mumbled, mispronounced, misused, misspoken, offensive, insensitive or inappropriate words, with replacements that could come from internet search, Digit and WION reported. CXOToday said the examples include colloquial terms such as "y'all" and idioms such as "bite the bullet," and that viewer profiles could include age, known languages and location.

The application also appears to anticipate questions about accuracy. According to Digit, it suggests that the original audio and video could be recorded and stored as a reference. WION reported that Microsoft had not commented on the patent. A patent application does not mean a company plans to release a product.

Coverage of the filing focused on what it could mean for trust in live media. Digit noted that viewers receiving different versions of the same speech may not know what the speaker actually said, and that regional expressions and accents could be filtered out. WION and CXOToday both linked the technology to the wider problem of deepfakes and disinformation, including the risk of altered political speeches.

The most practical uses in the filing, such as dubbing a live event into another language with matching lip movements, address a real need for global audiences. The harder question is the per-viewer design. Today, a live broadcast is a shared record of what someone said. A system that quietly adjusts that record for each viewer, even with good intentions, would make it harder to agree on what was actually said, which is why the stored original described in the filing would matter if the idea ever reached a product.
Watch for whether any live translation or speech cleanup feature with lip matching appears in Microsoft products such as Teams, and whether it labels edited speech for viewers.
